chunks.text: 2.2 Optimization methods The optimization method estimates transformation parameters by maximizing or minimizing the similarity metric. Gradient-based methods [ 24 ] , such as gradient descent [ 36 ] or Adam [ 21 ] , update the transformation based on the local partial derivatives of the similarity metric. They are computationally efficient but can easily get caught in local optima instead of finding the best overall solution. Population-based methods [ 33 ] , such as Evolution strategies (ES) [ 37 ] or particle swarm optimization (PSO) [ 19 , 39 ] , evaluate multiple candidate solutions across the search space. They are less likely to become trapped in local optima but generally require greater computational cost due to increased sampling. 3 Materials and methods 3.1 Tissue preparation This study used transgenic zebrafish that express green fluorescent protein (GFP) in endothelial cells (primarily blood vessels). Tg(kdrl:eGFP) zebrafish embryos were collected immediately after fertilization and incubated in their culture dishes containing E3 media (5 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM C ​ a ​ C ​ l 2 CaCl_{2} , and 0.33 mM M ​ g ​ S ​ O 4 MgSO_{4} in distilled water) at 29°C. At 20 hours post fertilization (HPF), the health of the embryos was checked with a brightfield microscope (Stemi 508, Carl Zeiss AG, Germany). Healthy embryos were then examined with an epifluorescence microscope (Axioscope 5, Carl Zeiss AG) to confirm fluorescence expression. Zebrafish were anesthetized using tricane during imaging. A 20X stock solution of tricaine (MS-222, TMS, tricaine methanesulfonate) was diluted to 1X before use. A single fluorescent zebrafish embryo was selected for imaging and anesthetized to prevent movement during imaging by being transferred to a culture dish containing 0.02% tricaine in E3 media. The chorion was manually removed from the embryo to enable clear visualization while imaging.

A concentration of 0.3% low-melting point agarose was used to maintain the sample positioning during imaging, while still allowing growth. Tricaine was mixed into the warm agarose solution to reach a final working concentration of 0.02%. The zebrafish embryo, along with the tricaine-agarose mixture was drawn up and pipetted into a glass cuvette, which was mounted on the sample stage for imaging. Images of the same embryo were acquired every 30 minutes from 21 HPF – 48 HPF. Additional tricaine/E3 was pipetted into the cuvette throughout the experiment to maintain sample anesthesia. 3.2 Image acquisition Images were acquired using a custom optical coherence tomography (OCT) and light sheet (LS) multimodal system (OCT+LS) [ 20 ] . LS excitation was produced using a 488 nm laser focused through a low numerical aperture objective (iChrome MLE, Toptica Photonics Inc., Farmington, NY). A scanning mirror was used to sweep the beam across the sample to produce a light sheet with a thickness of ∼ \sim 11 μ \mu m. Fluorescence emission was collected using a (NA = 0.8) 16 × \times water-dipping objective (N16LWD-PF, Nikon Corporation) and passed through a 520 ± \pm 5 nm bandpass filter to a digital camera (C11440-22CU, Hamamatsu). This provided a transverse resolution of 2.1 µm and a field of view of 1.81 mm × \times 1.81 mm. OCT used a swept source laser with a central wavelength of 1051 nm, 109 nm bandwidth, 100 kHz sweep rate, and incident power at the sample 6 mW. The system was based on a Michelson interferometer with a sensitivity of 100.1 dB and a 6.9 dB sensitivity roll-off over 4.1 mm. The axial and the lateral resolutions of OCT were 7.6 µm and 14.9 µm, respectively. The OCT beam passed through the polarization beam splitter, with one beam directed to the reference mirror and the other combined with the LS beam. The LS and OCT beams were aligned such that the excitation sheet and OCT beam lay in the same plane, allowing co-registration.

3.3 OCT+LS imaging constraints We define the shared OCT+LS coordinate system such that the z z axis corresponds to the excitation direction for both modalities (Figure 1 a). However, the collected OCT and LS images have different sampling rates (voxel sizes) along each axis due to physical constraints of the modalities. Since the OCT and LS excitation beams share an optical path, the x ​ z xz plane for both modalities is closely aligned and they share a sample rate along the y y axis ( 5 µ ​ m 5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} per voxel). The x ​ z xz plane coincides with the focal plane for the LS emission objective; therefore the z z and x x sampling rates for LS are isotropic ( 0.95 µ ​ m 0.95\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} ). The z z and x x sampling rates for OCT depend on the depth sampling of each A-line generated by the swept-source interferometric acquisition and the galvanometer scan spacing across the imaging plane, respectively (Figure 1 b). To register both modalities, we rely on constrained optimization. We first rescaled both images using their known voxel sizes. Because the OCT and LS paths are closely aligned, it is within the x ​ z xz plane that major misalignments can occur. These include a translation 𝐭 \mathbf{t} within the x ​ z xz plane and a rotation θ \theta along the y y axis (Figure 1 d). Although the OCT and LS excitation beams are designed to be co-planar, in practice there is always some unavoidable alignment error. To account for this, we allowed some constrained registration along the y y axis, as well as constrained rotations along the z z and x x axes. 3.4 Registration metrics This study evaluated several similarity metrics S ⁡ ( B 1 , B 2 ) S(B_{1},B_{2}) to compare two images B 1 B_{1} and B 2 B_{2} . These include MIND, SSD, NMI, and NCC (Section 2.1 ), for OCT+LS alignment.

Each metric was first evaluated using manually aligned registrations as ground truth (GT) and the corresponding similarity scores were recorded. The same metrics were then applied and the optimized similarity values were recorded and compared with the GT (Figure 3 ). Although some metrics achieved higher optimized scores during automatic registration, these values did not consistently correspond to visually correct alignment. Registration accuracy was further evaluated using mean target registration error (mTRE) (Figure 4 ). NCC demonstrated the most consistent performance, achieving the lowest mTRE values among the evaluated metrics. To further evaluate robustness, the same metrics were tested under constrained registration conditions across increasing translation bounds (0.5–2 mm) and rotation bounds ( 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} – 40 ∘ 40^{\circ} ). Figure 5 shows the visual alignment results at the smallest search range, and Figure 6 shows the corresponding mTRE across all evaluated bounds. NCC maintained reliable visual alignment and achieved the lowest mean mTRE across all search ranges, demonstrating robustness to the choice of PSO bounds. Therefore, NCC was selected as the primary similarity metric for OCT+LS alignment. NCC achieves the lowest mean mTRE across all evaluated PSO search ranges. 3.5 Optimization We tested four optimization algorithms for multimodal and temporal registration: Differential evolution (DE) [ 8 ] , Simulated annealing (SA) [ 11 ] , ES [ 26 ] , and PSO.

We found that PSO achieved higher NCC values compared with the other methods, indicating improved alignment quality (Figure 7 ). Furthermore, the convergence of mTRE over time demonstrated that PSO converged faster and reached lower registration errors than the other optimization algorithms(Figure 8 ). Therefore, PSO was selected as the primary optimization method for the registration. Fig 7: Comparison of optimization methods for aligning multimodal data with the NCC metric. OCT was selected for temporal registration because it provided consistent structural features across time points. The resulting transformation for each time point was subsequently applied to the corresponding LS volume (Figure 10 ), preserving the spatial correspondence established during pairwise registration. Substantial changes in sample orientation and spatial position due to repositioning during imaging and embryo growth required a coarse prealignment step before PSO optimization (Section 3.5 ). The OCT volume acquired at time t + 1 {t+1} was subjected to candidate flips and rotations within the XZ plane, and the translation for each candidate was estimated using NCC.

The candidate yielding the highest similarity to the OCT volume at time t {t} was used to initialize the registration. This initial transformation was refined using the rigid registration framework described in Section ( 3.7 ). Applying this procedure sequentially across consecutive time points mapped all OCT volumes into a common longitudinal coordinate system. Finally, the temporal transformations were transferred to the corresponding LS volumes using the pairwise OCT+LS relationships, preserving the multimodal alignment established at each time point. The longitudinal registration results are shown in Figure ( 11 ). The first row shows pairwise OCT+LS registration at each time point, followed by the sequential registration results in the XZ, YZ, and YX planes, demonstrating that multimodal alignment was maintained in the common longitudinal coordinate system. Following rows show sequential registration between time points in the YZ, ZX, and XY planes, respectively. 4 Conclusion The proposed framework provides a fully-automated approach for registering longitudinal OCT+LS images without manual landmark selection, a pre-existing segmentation, or feature correspondences between modalities. Unlike conventional feature-based methods, which can perform poorly when OCT and LS images contain different structural and molecular information, this approach uses image similarity and the physical constraints of the imaging system to achieve consistent alignment across modalities and developmental time points. The registered volumes allow tissue morphology captured by OCT to be directly compared with fluorescence information captured by LS.

This enables longitudinal studies of how environmental exposures, such as alcohol and micro or nanoplastics [ 15 ] , affect structural development and molecular expression in living zebrafish embryos. Future work will extend this framework to additional transgenic zebrafish and fluorescent labels that highlight different cell types, proteins, and biological processes. Applying this method will allow the relationships between tissue morphology and a broader range of molecular processes to be investigated throughout development. Future studies may also incorporate deformable registration to account for localized anatomical changes that cannot be fully represented by rigid transformations. The source code for the proposed implementation is available on GitHub (https://github.com/Mahshid-Babeli/octls-registration) with sample data sets available Zenodo [ 3 ] .
